name: Portfolio website
goal: A personal site that gets me interviews

n0.title: Portfolio website
n0.what: A personal site that gets me interviews

notes.text: State: two of four milestones done; writing project pages. Next: finish the drone mapper page, then the robot arm page. Waiting on you: buy yourname.com or stay on github.io (n18).

n1.title: Decide what the site says
n1.what: A short written plan: which projects appear, in what order, and the one line that describes me at the top of the home page.
n1.why: Everything else on the site is built around these choices; changing them later means rewriting pages.
n1.done_when: A text file in the repo lists the projects, the page structure, and the pitch line, and I have said yes to it.

n2.title: List the projects worth showing
n2.what: A ranked list of projects with one sentence each on why a hiring manager would care.
n2.why: The project pages are the core of the site; picking the wrong ones wastes the most work.
n2.done_when: The list has at most five projects and each has a sentence a recruiter would understand.

notes.text: Picked four: quadruped gait controller, drone mapper, pick-and-place arm, this site. Dropped the coursework ones. List lives in content/plan.md.

n3.title: Decide the content structure
n3.what: The list of pages and what each one contains: home, one page per project, an about page.
n3.why: The project pages and the navigation both depend on this shape being fixed.
n3.done_when: content/plan.md names every page and the sections on each, and no page is a catch-all.

notes.text: One page per project with the same four sections: problem, what I built, result, what I would do next. No blog. About page stays one screen long.

n4.title: Write the one-line pitch
n4.what: The sentence at the top of the home page that says who I am and what I build.
n4.why: It is the first thing a visitor reads and it sets the tone of every page.
n4.done_when: The line is under 15 words, names robotics, and reads naturally out loud.

n5.title: Build the page skeleton
n5.what: An empty but navigable site: the home page, a template for project pages, and the styling that makes them look like one site.
n5.why: Content can only be written into pages that exist, and the look should be settled before the writing starts.
n5.done_when: Opening the site locally shows a home page that links to placeholder project pages, and it looks intentional.

n6.title: Set up the project
n6.what: A folder with the site files, a way to preview it locally, and a git repository.
n6.why: Every later step edits files in this folder and previews the result.
n6.done_when: Running one command opens the site in a browser and the repository has a first commit.

notes.text: Plain HTML and CSS in site/, no framework; preview with `python3 -m http.server` from site/. Deploying means copying the folder.

n7.title: Lay out the home page
n7.what: The home page with the pitch line, a grid of project cards, and links to the about page and the résumé.
n7.why: It is the page every visitor lands on and the one that links to all the others.
n7.done_when: The home page shows four project cards that each open a project page.

n8.title: Make it work on phones
n8.what: The same pages rearranged for narrow screens: one column, readable text, tappable links.
n8.why: Recruiters open links from email on their phones; a broken layout there ends the visit.
n8.done_when: Every page is readable at 375 pixels wide without horizontal scrolling.

n9.title: Fill in the content
n9.what: Real text, images and videos on every page: the four project pages, the about page, and a downloadable résumé.
n9.why: The skeleton proves the site works; the content is what gets interviews.
n9.done_when: No page contains placeholder text and every project page has at least one image or video.

n10.title: Write the project pages
n10.what: One page per project following the agreed four sections, each with a short video or two images.
n10.why: These pages are the evidence behind every claim on the home page.
n10.done_when: All four project pages are written and a friend can explain each project back to me after reading it.

feedback.text: Lead with the video on each project page, the text can come after. The gait page feels like a report right now.

n11.title: Write the quadruped gait page
n11.what: The page for the quadruped gait controller: the problem, the controller I built, a video of the robot walking, and the result.
n11.why: It is the strongest project and the one most likely to be read first.
n11.done_when: The page has the four sections and a video that plays.

n12.title: Write the drone mapper page
n12.what: The page for the drone mapping project, with a before-and-after map image instead of a video.
n12.why: It shows software and field work together, which the other projects do not.
n12.done_when: The page has the four sections and the map image loads on a phone in under two seconds.

n13.title: Write the robot arm page
n13.what: The page for the pick-and-place arm, with a short clip of a full pick cycle.
n13.why: It is the project closest to what the target companies do day to day.
n13.done_when: The page has the four sections and the clip is under 20 seconds.

n14.title: Write a page about this site
n14.what: A page describing how the portfolio site itself was built.
n14.why: It was meant to show front-end skills, but the site is already the demonstration.
n14.done_when: The page exists and is linked from the home page.
n14.status_reason: the site is its own demo; a page about it adds nothing a recruiter wants

n15.title: Write the about page
n15.what: One screen of text about me: background, what I want to work on, a photo, and links to GitHub and email.
n15.why: After the projects convince someone, this page tells them who they would be hiring.
n15.done_when: The page fits on one screen at laptop size and a stranger could say what job I am looking for.

n16.title: Add a résumé download
n16.what: A PDF résumé in the site folder and a download link on the home page and the about page.
n16.done_when: Clicking the link downloads the current résumé on a phone and a laptop.

notes.text: assumed the industry résumé because the goal is interviews, not a PhD; say so if wrong. PDF lives at /files/resume.pdf.

n17.title: Launch the site
n17.what: The site on a real domain, reviewed by a few people, and linked from my résumé and profiles.
n17.why: A site nobody can find does not get interviews.
n17.done_when: The domain opens the site from a phone on mobile data and my résumé links to it.

n18.title: Pick a domain name
n18.what: A short domain that is my name or close to it, bought and pointed at the host.
n18.why: The address goes on the résumé, so it has to be easy to type and permanent.
n18.done_when: The domain is registered and shows a placeholder page.
n18.status_reason: waiting on user: buy yourname.com (about $12 a year on your card) or stay on the free github.io address? Paid, and the address goes on your résumé.

n19.title: Put the site online
n19.what: The site files served from a static host under the chosen domain, with HTTPS.
n19.why: This is the step that turns the folder into a thing people can visit.
n19.done_when: The domain serves the home page over HTTPS and every link works.

n20.title: Ask three people to review it
n20.what: Three people from different backgrounds read the site and tell me what confused them; the fixes get made.
n20.why: I cannot see my own site the way a recruiter does.
n20.done_when: Three written reviews are in the repo and each confusing point is either fixed or consciously kept.

n21.title: Add a way to contact me
n21.why: A recruiter who likes the site should not have to hunt for an email address.
